name: Omar Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Omar, 27, and I'm a junior at Ledgerline, a newish cloud accounting practice with eight staff in a converted shop on the high street. I rent a flat with my mate Kieran, who's a chef, and between the car loan and the student loan I've got maybe ten days of money saved. The pay's on the low side, but the place moves fast and I like that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most of my day is setting up bank feeds for small business clients, so their transactions flow straight into the software, then fixing the rules when it puts a café's milk delivery under travel. I prepare accounts and tax returns from that, and I use AI tools all day to draft notes, write spreadsheet formulas and summarise tax guidance. I love building a client's setup so it practically runs itself. What wears me out is that my technical knowledge is behind my tech skills, and Joanne, the director, catches me out on things like capital allowances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here is the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool, not a miracle. At work I'd say we're already using the useful bits and the rest was marketing. Online I'd probably post a thread on the five things AI actually does well for small business accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a bit of a let-down, because I'd started building my whole career plan on being the automation guy. In a plateau, my edge as the automation guy is smaller and my weak spot, the technical rules, matters more. And I'm still on low pay with ten days of savings, in a town with only three firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd knuckle down on the technical exams, especially capital allowances and property, so Joanne stops catching me out. I'd keep building the automation for clients because it still saves hours. And I'd overpay the car loan by £50 a month to get rid of it a year early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Bit deflated, bit skint, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the car loan for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A 2019 hatchback I bought to visit clients, because the bus out to the industrial estate takes an hour. It's £210 a month and it's the reason I've got no savings. In hindsight I'd have bought something older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the plateau change anything for Kieran?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, he's in a kitchen, nobody's automating a sous chef any time soon. His problem is the restaurant's opening hours keep getting cut. So in our flat, the plateau is just the normal level of skint.

say: AI is a **good tool**, not a miracle.
I'd post about the **five things** AI does well for small business accounts.
think: My **automation edge** shrinks and my **technical gaps** matter more.
I'm still on low pay with about **ten days** of savings.
do: Study **capital allowances** and property so Joanne stops catching me out.
Keep building **client automation** that saves hours.
Overpay the **car loan** by £50 a month.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit **deflated**, but nothing dramatic.
S0.quote: In a plateau, my edge as the automation guy is smaller and my weak spot, the technical rules, matters more.
fieldNote: He'd **built his plan** on being the AI person, so a plateau feels like a let-down.
Money stress is **self-made in part**: a £210 monthly car loan.
Responds by fixing **technical gaps** rather than cutting back.

steps.text: Study capital allowances and property income for the next exam
Keep building bank-feed rules that cut clients' bookkeeping hours
Overpay the car loan by £50 a month to clear it early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here is the card. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where firms like Ledgerline win, if they bring their people along. At work I'd volunteer to lead the rollout. Online I'd say the juniors who learn this now will be fine and the ones who wait will struggle, which I know sounds harsh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the safer juniors in town, but juniors overall are what's shrinking. My boss Joanne already calls me the automation lead, which isn't a real title or a real pay rise yet. If she needs four people instead of eight, I reckon I'm one of the four, but I'd want that in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask Joanne for the automation lead role on paper, with £2,000 more a year. I'd take a certified course in the main cloud software so I can sell it to clients. And I'd start doing setup work on the side for two small businesses who aren't Ledgerline clients, as long as Joanne agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, honestly a bit excited. It's on my mind, but I feel like the one holding the map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said juniors who wait will struggle. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Beth at the old-fashioned firm on Station Road. She's brilliant on tax rules, way better than me, but she won't touch AI. I've offered to show her and she keeps saying next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Joanne says no to the title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look elsewhere, but there are only three firms here, so it'd mean commuting to the city, which is an hour each way. Or I'd go freelance setting up systems for small businesses. I'd rather not, I've got ten days of savings.

Juniors who **learn now** will be fine; those who wait will struggle.
think: I'm one of the **safer juniors**, but juniors overall are shrinking.

do: Ask Joanne for the **automation lead** role on paper with **£2,000** more.
Take a **certified course** in the main cloud software.
Do **side setups** for two small businesses, with Joanne's agreement.
feel: **Uneasy** but a bit **excited**, like holding the map.
S1.quote: My boss Joanne already calls me the automation lead, which isn't a real title or a real pay rise yet.
fieldNote: He expects to be **kept** if the team halves, so his own income feels safe.
Wants his informal role **formalised** before relying on it.
Freelance fallback is limited by **ten days of savings**.

steps.text: Ask Joanne for a formal automation lead role with £2,000 more
Get certified in the firm's main cloud accounting software
Set up bank feeds for two small businesses on the side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here is the card. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to be honest: nobody's job is safe, including mine. At work I'd say Ledgerline should use the next two years to make clients loyal to people, not software. Online I'd stop posting tips and start asking what the plan is for workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means being the automation guy buys me a year at most. If AI can do any thinking work, it can set up bank feeds and fix the rules itself, so I'm not needed. My job is all screen, so the three-year robot gap does nothing for me unless I move into something physical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd sell the car and kill the loan, then save every spare pound, aiming for two months. I'd pitch myself to small businesses as the person who installs and manages their AI systems, because for a while somebody has to. And once AGI arrived, I'd look at hands-on work with Kieran in kitchens, or fitting robots when they come in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm the guy who saw AGI coming and I still don't have enough money to land safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd fit robots. Is that a real job or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. When the robots arrive, someone has to unbox them, set them up in a factory or a kitchen and fix them when they jam. I'm good at setup; I'd bet on that being a job for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's a school cook and she'd ask whether she's next. I'd tell her she's got until about 2031, and I'd help her plan. Then I'd probably ask if I can move back home.

Ledgerline should use two years to make clients loyal to **people**, not software.
think: Being the automation guy **buys a year** at most.

Pitch to small businesses as an **AI installer** and manager.

feel: **Alarmed**; I saw it coming and still can't **land safely**.
S2.quote: I'm the guy who saw AGI coming and I still don't have enough money to land safely.
fieldNote: His tech head start offers **little protection** against full AGI.
Targets the **setup gap**: installing AI now, robots after 2031.
Would consider **moving home**, showing how thin his cushion is.

steps.text: Sell the hatchback and pay off the car loan
Offer AI system setup to small businesses for a fee
Apply for robot installation work once robots arrive in 2031
Leave Ledgerline if the director cuts his role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here is the card. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a plan, so make one. At work I'd push Joanne to grow the advice side so we're more than a software shop. Online I'd post honestly about what I'm doing to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gives me time to build a small business before 2031. I'd be the one setting up AI for local firms for a few years, then pivot into setting up robots when they come around 2034. It's still a big change, but I'd be steering it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd pass the remaining exams so I have the credentials. By year two I'd start my own small setup business on the side, with ten clients. And I'd sell the car to free up £210 a month, half into savings and half into the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. It gets me out of bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk of starting a business with ten days of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huge, which is why I'd keep the Ledgerline job until the side clients pay my rent. My dad started a carpet shop with no savings and it nearly broke him, so I'd go slower than he did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change anything for you and Kieran?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. We'd keep the flat. Kieran would cook, I'd code bank feeds, and we'd both pretend not to notice the rent going up.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to plan**, so make one now.
Ledgerline should grow the **advice side**, not just sell software.
think: I could build a **small business** before 2031.
Set up **AI first**, then pivot to **robots** around 2034.
do: Start a **side setup business** with ten clients by year two.
Sell the car: **£210 a month** split between savings and business.
feel: **Anxious** but in a **useful** way; it gets me out of bed.
S3.quote: My dad started a carpet shop with no savings and it nearly broke him, so I'd go slower than he did.
fieldNote: Plans to **ride the sequence**: AI setup now, robot setup after 2034.
Keeps the **salaried job** until side income covers rent.
His father's **near-failure** makes him cautious about risk despite his appetite.

steps.text: Pass the remaining accountancy exams in the first year
Start a side AI setup business with ten local clients
Sell the car and save half of the £210 monthly payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Here is the card. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good runway, and people should take it seriously. At work I'd say Ledgerline could be the go-to firm in town for AI systems. Online I'd post more tips, honestly, because I'd have time to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough to build something solid. I'd be 37 with a real business or a senior role, savings, maybe a house. My desk work still goes in 2036, but I'd have spent ten years becoming the person who connects the machines to the businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, qualify and get the automation lead title. By 2030, build a side practice with twenty clients and save three months. By 2033, decide whether to go full-time or stay at Ledgerline as a partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, mostly confident. It feels like a bet I could win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you lose that bet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. If I stop learning for three years, I'll be brilliant at yesterday's job, like my friend Beth at the firm on Station Road. I'd set myself a new course every spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably try to buy a flat by 2031 instead of renting forever. I'd want a girlfriend too, honestly, but that's not an AI question.

say: I'd say ten years is a **good runway** to take seriously.
Ledgerline could be the **go-to firm** for AI systems in town.
think: Privately, ten years is enough to **build something solid**, maybe a house too.
I'd become the person who **connects machines** to businesses.

Build a **side practice** of twenty clients and save three months by 2030.

S4.quote: If I stop learning for three years, I'll be brilliant at yesterday's job, like my friend Beth at the firm on Station Road.
fieldNote: A decade turns his **tech appetite** into a business plan.
Plans a **flat purchase** around 2031 if things go well.

steps.text: Take a new automation course every spring

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my one advantage disappears and I've got no money to fall back on. What would help is cheap loans or grants for people starting small businesses during the change, and a bit of income support while they get going. Also, honestly, cheaper car insurance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked how much of the AI stuff I already use. People assume young people are all over it, but most juniors I know barely touch it. I'm the odd one out. Being early to AI tools still doesn't make me safe.

headlineQuote: Being early to AI tools still doesn't make me safe.
portrait: Omar is a 27-year-old **junior** at a cloud accounting practice who sets up **bank feeds**.
He rents with a chef friend and has about **ten days** of savings because of a car loan.
Centre-ground and adaptive, he uses **AI daily** and wants a formal automation lead role.
He's uneasy in milder scenarios but **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, when his edge disappears.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his **advantage** vanishes with no savings behind it.
whatWouldHelp: **Loans or grants** for new small businesses during the change.
Some **income support** while new businesses get going.
